books.section: Topic 7.7 1920s: Innovations in Communication and Technology

stimulus.text:
United States military aircraft production (Army Air Forces official history):

| Year | 1940 | 1941 | 1942 | 1943 | 1944 |
| Military aircraft built | 6,086 | 26,277 | 47,836 | 85,898 | 96,318 |

Context: In 1913 Henry Ford's moving assembly line at Highland Park cut the time to assemble a Model T chassis from more than twelve hours to under two hours, and the Model T's price fell as production rose. In World War II, the federal War Production Board directed factories to war work, and American industry built about 300,000 military aircraft in all between July 1940 and August 1945.
stimulus.source_note: Aircraft figures are from the Army Air Forces official history (Craven and Cate, The Army Air Forces in World War II, vol. VI). Context drawn from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topics 7.7 and 7.12.

source: original; stimulus drawn from book-grounded paraphrases, tables, and photographs (see source_note)
stem: How did World War II aircraft production build on the 1913 assembly line?

options.text: Aircraft factories abandoned the assembly line entirely in 1940
options.misconception: The passage says production was transformed into a mass-production industry, not that the line was abandoned.

options.text: Mass-production methods from car factories were scaled up for warplanes
Car factories stopped using assembly lines after 1913 entirely
options.misconception: Car factories kept using assembly lines; the passage says the method spread, not that it stopped.

options.text: Aircraft production relied only on handcrafted work by skilled artisans
options.misconception: The passage says aircraft manufacture changed from handwork to mass production.

rationales.A: Background from the books: wartime aircraft factories used assembly-line mass production, not handwork.
rationales.B: Ford's moving line cut chassis assembly to under two hours, and wartime factories used the same mass-production methods to build 96,318 planes in 1944.
rationales.C: Background from the books: assembly lines stayed at the heart of car making long after 1913.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the passage says aircraft manufacture was transformed from handwork to mass production.
rationales.general:
1. Find the 1913 method in the context: a moving assembly line that cut chassis work to under two hours.
2. Find the wartime result in the table: aircraft output rose from 6,086 in 1940 to 96,318 in 1944.
3. That rise needed factory methods that could turn out planes by the thousand.
4. Background: the car industry's mass-production methods were scaled up for warplanes.
Remember: a method that works for cars can be scaled up for planes.
